title: Spectral scalar curvature and uniform Urysohn width
abstract: For every n ≥ 4, a complete connected smooth Riemannian n-manifold without boundary satisfying -4\Delta+\mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}\nolimits \ge1 as a quadratic-form inequality admits a continuous map to a simplicial complex of dimension at most n-2 whose entire fibers have diameter bounded only in terms of n. The bound is measured in the original metric. This extends the uniform Urysohn width theorem from a pointwise scalar-curvature lower bound to a spectral lower bound.
result_title: Spectral scalar curvature, Urysohn width, and macroscopic dimension
subject: Differential geometry
overall_assessment:
The paper reduces a uniform bound on the Urysohn $(n-2)$-width under the spectral bound $-4\Delta_g+\mathrm{Scal}_g\ge1$ to a partition theorem (Theorem 2.1) that it imports from a companion manuscript by the same author.

The analytic sections are correct as far as I can verify. I recomputed these items and found no error: the supersolution identity of Lemma 3.1; the angle equation and the barrier and cutoff estimates of Lemmas 3.3 and 3.4; the scalar comparison of Lemma 3.5; the square completions and the constant $C(n)=100n+203$ of Proposition 3.2; the inverse derivatives and all bounds of the pressure law (Proposition 4.1); the slope bounds, the two curvature cases, the cutoff and the distance gain $\sqrt{1+.11^2}>L_*=1.004$ of Lemma 5.1; the trace invariant of Lemma 6.1; the scale restoration $L_*^2(1-(n+1)\delta)>1$ and the warp energy bound $\frac1{10}$ in the proof of Theorem 1.1. The ten sub-agents for these sections also reported no finding.

The weak point is the import. Theorem 2.1 contains the full topological content of Theorem 1.1, and for $\mathrm{Scal}_g\ge1$ it already includes an open question of Gromov for $n\ge4$. The paper does not prove it. The paper also uses it for data outside the setting of the source (a drift with both signs and no bound, a metric $h$ from a new graph construction, a very large scale $D=WR_0$) and supports this only with assertions about the source. Therefore Theorem 1.1 is conditional: if Theorem 2.1 holds as stated, then Theorem 1.1 holds. The abstract and the theorem statement must say this, or the paper must include a proof of Theorem 2.1 for the data that Section 6 gives.

comments.title: Theorem 1.1 is conditional on an imported theorem that the paper does not prove
comments.quote: We use this theorem as an imported result.  It follows from
comments.explanation:
Sections 3 to 6 prove only this: from the spectral bound there are a complete metric $h\ge g$ and a drift $t$ with $\mathcal D(h,t)\ge\frac12$ and $\mathrm{dist}_h(A_i,B_i)>L_i$, and then log warps with $R(h,(p_\alpha))\ge\frac25$. No step there gives a map to a complex or decreases a dimension. The full passage from the data $(h,(p_\alpha))$ to a map $f:M\to K$ with $\dim K\le n-2$ and fibers of $g$-diameter at most $4D+2$ is Theorem 2.1, and its only source is \cite{OpenAIWidth}, a companion manuscript by the same author.

The uniform bound on the Urysohn $(n-2)$-width for $\mathrm{Scal}_g\ge1$ in dimensions $n\ge4$ is the question of Gromov that Section 1.1 describes. Because $\mathrm{Scal}_g\ge1$ implies the spectral bound, Theorem 1.1 contains that question as a special case. Thus the sentence in the abstract, "This extends the uniform Urysohn width theorem", refers to a theorem that a reader cannot find in the literature.

Theorem 2.1 is also not one numbered result of the source. The text says that it "follows from" Lemma 6.1, Proposition 6.6, Proposition 7.1 and Equation (7.14) there, and gives the derivation only as a description in prose.

What I verified in this paper is correct: the warp formula for $R(h,(p_\alpha))$; the value $\frac14+1.12\cdot\frac1{20}=.306\le\frac25$; the fiber bound $4D+2$ from $d_g(x,q(x))<1$ and a common coordinate $a_i=1$; the scalar comparison of Lemma 3.5; the three square completions and $C(n)=100n+203$ in Proposition 3.2; the derivative identities and all five bounds of Proposition 4.1; the two slope ranges and the length comparison $\sqrt{1+.11^2}>1.004$ in Lemma 5.1; the invariant $\mathcal D(H,z)\ge c+\Lambda V(z)$ and the factor $L_*^2(1-(n+1)\delta)>1$ in Section 6. These steps all end at the hypotheses of Theorem 2.1. The correct summary of the paper is: if Theorem 2.1 holds as stated, then Theorem 1.1 holds. The abstract and the statement of Theorem 1.1 must say this, or the paper must contain a proof of Theorem 2.1.

comments.title: Theorem 2.1 is used for data outside the setting of the cited source
comments.quote: ends.  Thus the initial data need no uniform bounds on the geometry
comments.explanation:
Theorem 2.1 puts no condition on the sign or size of $P=\sum_\alpha p_\alpha$, on the weight $e^P\,\mathrm d\mathrm{vol}_h$, on $\mathrm{Scal}_g$, or on the relation between $h$ and $g$ other than $h\ge g$. The paper itself shows that the data of the source are more special. Sections 4, 5 and 6 each say that the pressure law, the local stretching and the round argument of the source must be adapted "to allow the drift to take either sign". Thus the drift of the source has one sign.

In the proof of Theorem 1.1 the log warps are $p_\alpha=-\varphi_\nu t/m_\nu$, so $P=-t$ has both signs and no bound, $|\mathrm dP|_h$ has no bound, and the numbers $m_\nu$ have no uniform bound on $M$. The metric $h$ also contains the graph term $\mathrm du\otimes\mathrm du$ of Proposition 3.2, which the source does not use. For the import to be valid, Sections 6 and 7 of the source must use nothing about $(h,(p_\alpha))$ except the two inequalities $\mathrm{dist}_h(A_i,B_i)>10+2\pi\sqrt{2/p_i^*}$ and $R(h,(p_\alpha))\ge\frac25$.

The paper does not prove this. Each sentence between "The countable version" and "conclusions of the imported construction" is an assertion about the source, and the word "Thus" follows from none of them in a way that a reader can check. These points stay open:

1. The paper removes the hypothesis $\mathrm{Scal}_g\ge1$ only for Lemma 6.1 of the source. It says nothing about Propositions 6.4, 6.6, 7.1 or Equation (7.14), which give the map $q$, the bound $n-2$ on the number of intermediate coordinates, and the fiber bound.
2. The product cylinders are not compact. A reason is necessary why existence and compactness for the weighted variational problem hold when $e^P$ has no bound from above or below.
3. For infinite $I$, $\sum_i p_i^*<\infty$ gives $p_i^*\to0$, so the necessary separations $10+2\pi\sqrt{2/p_i^*}$ go to infinity.
4. The threshold $\frac14+1.12\sum_i p_i^*$ is the "initial" requirement of one lemma. The paper does not show that the later steps of the induction use no more of the scalar reserve when the initial drift is not zero.

This finding is independent of the first one. If the source proves its theorem for $\mathrm{Scal}_g\ge1$ correctly, the use here can still be outside its range. The paper must quote a statement of the source that contains these data literally, or prove the passage.

comments.title: The validity of Theorem 2.1 for every $D\ge D_{\mathrm{nat}}(n)$ has no justification
comments.quote: the initial scale may be enlarged.
comments.explanation:
The proof of Theorem 1.1 uses Theorem 2.1 with $D=WR_0$, where $W\ge10^5$ and $\frac{R_0^2}{2}\ge C(n)+T^2$ with $C(n)=100n+203$. Thus $D$ is much larger than a natural scale of the problem, and the final constant is $C_n=4WR_0+2$.

The only support for the range $D\ge D_{\mathrm{nat}}(n)$ is the quoted phrase. The hypotheses of Theorem 2.1 are not invariant under scaling: the constants $10$, $2\pi\sqrt{2/p_i^*}$, $\frac25$ and the displacement bound $d_g(x,q(x))<1$ are absolute, while $A_i$ and $B_i$ change with $D$. Therefore monotonicity in $D$ is a real claim. It is not a consequence of a rescaling of $g$, because a rescaling also changes $R(h,(p_\alpha))$.

The paper must give the statement of the source that permits each $D\ge D_{\mathrm{nat}}(n)$, or prove it. Without this, the choice $D=WR_0$ in the proof of Theorem 1.1 has no support.

comments.title: The range $n\ge4$ with no upper limit comes only from the import
comments.quote: For each integer $n\ge4$, there is a finite number $D_{\mathrm{nat}}(n)>0$
comments.explanation:
Sections 3 to 6 do not use $n\ge4$. Lemma 3.1, Proposition 3.2 (the dimension enters only through $|J|^2\ge H^2/(n-1)$), Proposition 4.1, Lemma 5.1 (through $\epsilon\le1/(8n)$) and Lemma 6.1 (through $Q\le n$) hold for each $n\ge2$. Thus the full dependence of Theorem 1.1 on the dimension comes from Theorem 2.1.

Section 2 says that the cited construction separates $A_i$ from $B_i$ by hypersurfaces from a variational problem with weight $e^P\,\mathrm d\mathrm{vol}_h$. Minimizers of such problems are in general smooth only for $n\le7$. For $n\ge8$ an analysis of the singular set or a perturbation argument is necessary. The paper does not say how the import handles $n\ge8$.

I cannot see the cited proof, so this is a request for information and not a claim of an error. The paper should add one sentence on the regularity of the separating hypersurfaces in high dimensions.
